paragraphs: You can first observe whether you are willing to check dimensions, positions, colours and material records thoroughly and to recalculate when the layout changes. Interest also needs to be judged together with fine handwork, physical load and real site conditions.

If you are not comfortable with dust, kneeling, squatting and bending, lifting or continuous work, first learn about the target task and the training arrangements. Drawing on paper does not test site fitness; cutting, adhesive work, demolition and work at height must have the corresponding training and authority.

Hard tile setting, stone masonry, resilient flooring and carpet may all appear in construction, but the materials and finished products differ. Do not choose training on the strength of the single label fitter.

First do the M1 wall model on this page: draw 6 rows and 4 columns using 600×300 mm tiles; M2 changes the colour of two cells; M3 writes the stock and the no-construction handover. All data is fictitious and paper and pen or a form is enough.
How is it worth trying tile and stone setting first?

Use dimension and version records to test your interest: unify metres and millimetres, locate the rows and columns, calculate how many units each colour needs, then state the shortfall and unknown conditions. A willingness to correct errors supports learning more about the job but does not directly prove construction ability.
This is only an editorial experience for career exploration and cannot replace tool training, project permits, safety procedures, project acceptance or a health evaluation.

Behaviour worth observing further: a willingness to re-check cell by cell rather than only looking at the effect, keeping both the old and new drawings, and writing area, quantity, stock and shortfall separately. Unclear substrate or material conditions are clearly left as questions.

If you frequently ignore dimension units, treat different batches as the same material, or delete unconfirmed items to finish quickly, go back to checking and training first. A personality label or a pretty pattern cannot be used to infer suitability.

Check the colour and quantity change between M1 and M2, then see whether someone else could recompute M3. Record what you have done and the real tasks you have not yet encountered, and do not write a correct model as independent construction competence.

O*NET47-2044.00 is now titled Tile and Stone Setters, covering the installation of hard tile, stone and similar materials on building surfaces. The current slug and Chinese name are the locally frozen identity, and no single Chinese qualification certificate is inferred from the translated name.

Work inputs are drawings, surface dimensions, material specifications and site conditions. When a version or dimension conflict arises, first point out the specific location and units; missing joint width, substrate or detail requirements cannot be treated as approved conditions on your own.

First use the drawings and surface information to understand the layout and material requirements, then confirm the real process basis. The M1 model extracts only geometry and colour checking; cutting, waste and material suitability in actual construction are not determined by the model.

The main deliverables are installed and finished hard facing material, layout and joints, and the related material and change records. O*NET also lists marble, granite and precast terrazzo tasks; appearance does not mean the whole project is acceptable.

Measuring, marking and checking the layout with a level, square and straightedge are the task baseline. Readers can check rows and columns on paper; actual tool use, material processing and on-site positioning require training and the corresponding authority.

Setters communicate materials, drawings and progress with clients, site supervisors, suppliers and other trades. The clarifier, the executor and the acceptor follow the real project's division of labor, and the occupational title does not confer design or acceptance rights.

The latest BLS precise occupational preparation measure is no formal educational credential, no related work experience and long-term on-the-job training. It describes the typical US entry route and cannot support a conclusion that no training is needed in China or that seven days is enough to build.

The handover should state the drawing version, materials, whether work was carried out and the items to confirm. When cracking, replacement, substrate or interface problems arise, feed them back along the chain of responsibility, and the recorder does not declare acceptance on their own.

The following are two editorially defined internal task lines: tile facing layout and joints, and stone specifications and installation and finishing. A job need not cover all materials and locations; expanding tasks requires re-checking the training.

The US O*NET context involves handwork, accuracy, kneeling, squatting and bending and repetitive motions, and also notes that noise and contaminants need to be understood. Its group survey cannot describe the exposure level of every Chinese site or an individual's health status.

Sites and division of labor | residential and commercial new-build or renovation projects are organized by material and trade, and locations may be walls, floors, countertops and similar. Check the project size, employment relationship and the processes actually undertaken, and do not assume all jobs are the same.

Objects and tools | drawings, measuring tools, hard tile and stone and material records form the task background; O*NET lists CAD, estimating, spreadsheet and office software, which does not mean any particular software or AI tool is mandatory across the occupation.
The pace is set by the drawings, materials and process sequencing. Dimension or material changes must be explained promptly, and real construction steps cannot be arranged from the paper grid alone.

Time and load | first check kneeling, squatting and bending, lifting and rest. The merged BLS page notes that commercial sites may work evenings and weekends, which is not evidence that all jobs in this occupation work shifts.

Communication requires clear locations, units, versions and open items. Mark estimates, measurements, assumptions and others' confirmations separately so the next step does not mistake a draft for approved information.

Division of responsibility | on-site execution, safety management, substrate confirmation and project acceptance are set by the actual project. Chinese site entry and special tasks are checked against local task rules; OSHA serves only as US risk background.

Record quality | dimensions and materials match the drawing, version changes are traceable and missing items are not hidden. The model work sample only shows the calculation and recording process and does not prove cutting or project acceptance ability.

The US 47-2044 scope includes walls, floors, ceilings, countertops and some roofing; the actual materials, processes and authority of Chinese jobs must be confirmed separately.

Stonemasons 47-2022 focus on stone walls, piers and other masonry; this occupation installs hard facing material, and sharing the stone material does not mean the structural responsibility or training is the same.

47-3011 is the merged brickmason and tile setter helper role, and helping with materials, tools and clean-up is not proof of independent setting ability.
47-2161 plastering and stucco form continuous surfaces, whereas this occupation installs hard facing material; belonging to the same fit-out field does not make them directly interchangeable.

Distinguish the objects and outputs by hard facing material, stone masonry, resilient flooring, support tasks and plaster surfaces. Even on the same site, the responsibility, tools and training differ.

Check the location, working hours, whether evenings and weekends are possible, commuting and family arrangements. The BLS commercial scenario is merged background and does not mean every job in this occupation has the same schedule.

State the physical load and training boundaries: check kneeling, squatting, lifting, dust and tool conditions first. The model on this page requires no dangerous actions or contact with materials, and completing it does not prove physical fit.

values: Material | the M1 strip wall model

A fictitious wall 2.4 metres wide × 1.8 metres high, tiles 600 millimetres wide × 300 millimetres high, laid horizontally without rotation; the model ignores joint width, cutting, waste, substrate and details and is paper geometry only.

v1 has 6 rows and 4 columns, r1—r6 from top to bottom and c1—c4 from left to right. In each row c1 is blue and c2 to c4 are white; all 24 cells have a unit. Stock: white batch W1 20 units, blue batch B1 5 units, all fictitious and of the same specification; no delivery or actual setting.
Task | M1 to M3

In M1, draw v1 and calculate the rows and columns, area, total unit count, white and blue requirements and the stock difference. M2 changes only r3c2 and r4c2 from white to blue, leaving the other 22 cells unchanged as v2; the original strip rule is not restored, so keep v1 and recompute.

Reference | recomputation and handover for both versions

600 millimetres = 0.6 metres and 300 millimetres = 0.3 metres, so the width 2.4 ÷ 0.6 = 4 columns and the height 1.8 ÷ 0.3 = 6 rows, 24 cells in total; each cell is 0.18 square metres, total 4.32 square metres. In v1 there are 6 blue and 18 white; stock of 5 blue is 1 short and stock of 20 white leaves 2 over.

In v2 two white cells become blue: 16 white and 8 blue, with the total of 24 cells and 4.32 square metres unchanged; 20 white leaves 4 over and 5 blue is 3 short. M3 hands over v2, white W1 stock 20 needing 16 with 4 over, and blue B1 stock 5 needing 8 with 3 short; it cannot be written as fully stocked or already built, and the site conditions remain to be checked.
